chunks: "SI and PI are the two halves of making a high-speed board actually work.
Signal integrity is about whether a signal arrives at the receiver intact: the right voltage at the right time.
The things that can go wrong are reflections from impedance mismatches, ringing, crosstalk between traces, loss and distortion in the channel, timing jitter and skew, and ground bounce.
They all get worse as edges get faster, because the edge then sees every trace as a transmission line.

Power integrity is about delivering a clean, stable supply to the chips: DC drop through the planes and connectors, ripple from the regulator, and especially the transient droop when a processor or FPGA suddenly demands current.
The design target is a power distribution network whose impedance stays below a target of allowed voltage ripple divided by the transient current.
For a 1 volts rail with 3 percent ripple and a 10 amps step, that's 3 milliohms, from DC up to the frequencies the chip switches at.
You do that with the regulator, bulk capacitors, many ceramic decoupling capacitors, and the plane pair. They're linked.
Noise on the supply modulates driver and receiver timing, so it becomes jitter on the signal.
Switching currents flowing through shared ground and supply inductance disturb other signals.
And a signal that crosses a plane split has a broken return path, which is both an SI and a PI problem.
They matter because voltages are low, so noise margins are tens of millivolts, edges are fast, and currents are big.
A board that violates these rules may work on the bench and fail with temperature, or never boot at all."
